analysis.one_liner: Taxes 100% of interest and dividends on frozen Russian and Belarusian assets to fund Ukraine reconstruction.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 41–5 with bipartisan support, but the full House never voted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 100% tax on the interest and dividends that Russia and Belarus earn on assets the U.S. has frozen because of the invasion of Ukraine. That money would go into a new Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund for rebuilding, humanitarian aid, and economic recovery. It would also make it official U.S. policy to press allies around the world to send the returns on frozen Russian assets to Ukraine, since most of the roughly $300 billion in frozen Russian assets is held in Europe, not here.
analysis.who_benefits: The people of Ukraine, who would get reconstruction and humanitarian funding paid for out of income on Russia's own frozen assets rather than new U.S. taxpayer money. The U.S. Treasury would also gain the withheld tax revenue before it is transferred onward.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 100% tax on interest and dividends payable on Russian and Belarusian assets blocked under emergency sanctions powers, overriding the normal exemption for foreign governments and any treaty obligation [S3][S2].

Routes the tax revenue into a new Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund for rebuilding, humanitarian assistance, long-term economic growth, and transparent governance, with annual reports to Congress [S3][S2].

Declares U.S. policy that returns on Russian sovereign assets frozen by allies should go to Ukraine, authorizes $25 million for a special economic-recovery envoy, and directs the U.N. ambassador to press other countries to build mechanisms to transfer those returns [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: The Russian and Belarusian governments, which would lose all income earned on their frozen U.S. assets. Banks and asset managers holding those assets would lose that income stream and take on the job of withholding the full amount. Ordinary Americans bear essentially no direct cost, since the tax falls on foreign government income, though the treaty override could expose the U.S. to legal challenges or retaliation against American assets held abroad.
analysis.who_pays_short: Russia, Belarus, and banks holding frozen assets

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings note that less than 2% of the roughly $300 billion in frozen Russian sovereign assets is held in the United States, so the direct tax revenue would be small compared with Ukraine's needs; the bill's larger purpose is to set a diplomatic precedent for Europe to act [S3].

The tax applies 'without regard to any treaty obligation of the United States' [S3], which legal observers could fairly object to as a breach of U.S. treaty commitments that might invite retaliation against American assets held abroad or complicate allied cooperation on asset transfers.
Taxing income on frozen assets stops short of seizing the underlying assets, so the principal stays protected and Russia's wealth remains largely intact even under the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow but real step: it converts income on frozen Russian assets into Ukraine aid instead of leaving that income to accrue to Russia, at essentially no cost to U.S. taxpayers. Its limits are that the money involved is small because most frozen Russian assets sit in Europe, and the treaty override carries genuine legal and diplomatic risk. The heavy lift the bill envisions — getting allies to transfer returns on their own frozen Russian assets — depends entirely on diplomacy the bill can only urge, not compel.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee approved it 41–5 in December 2023, but House leadership never brought it up for a vote on the floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett (D-TX) introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, with a bipartisan list of original cosponsors including Republicans Reps. Joe Wilson, Don Bacon, Brian Fitzpatrick, and María Elvira Salazar [S3][S5].
It was referred to both the Foreign Affairs Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On December 13, 2023, the Ways and Means Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a vote of 41–5 [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never received a vote on the House floor, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Russia and Belarus keep earning tax-free income on their frozen U.S. assets, and the financial institutions managing those assets keep their business. Ukraine receives nothing from this funding route, and the diplomatic push to have allies transfer returns on frozen Russian assets goes nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Russia, Belarus, and banks managing frozen assets

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on December 13, 2023 and ordered the bill reported, as amended, 41–5.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and floor leadership, House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote on the House floor at any point after it was reported out of committee; the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 63 cosponsors split 52 Democrats and 11 Republicans, and cleared committee on a 41–5 vote; the obstacle was the absence of a floor vote, not recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Russian and Belarusian governments (holders of frozen sovereign assets)
industries.note: The bill would take 100% of the interest and dividends these governments earn on assets frozen in the U.S. and route the money to Ukraine's reconstruction. Because most frozen Russian assets are held in Europe, the direct hit is small, but the bill's real aim is to establish the precedent that frozen Russian wealth should pay for the war's damage.

industries.industry: Banks and asset managers holding frozen Russian assets
industries.note: These institutions would lose the income stream on the frozen assets they manage and would be legally responsible for withholding the entire amount. Their financial interest lies in the frozen assets continuing to earn and sit untouched, which is exactly what the bill would change.
